# Edible insects

For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the edible insects came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-edible-insects" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-edible-insects-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of edible insects, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Edible insects, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>36.6</td><td>61.8</td><td>104</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>36.6</td><td>61.8</td><td>104</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>6 reference units; 1 sampling family. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Holowaty et al. 2024</td><td>6</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for edible insects, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>Holowaty et al. 2024 is the only compatible sampling family for edible insects, as sold on this basis in the completed edible insects ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/holowaty2024-french-online-edible-insects-elements" class="internal" data-slug="sources/holowaty2024-french-online-edible-insects-elements" data-no-cite-meta>Holowaty et al. 2024</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach edible insects

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach edible insects comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Edible insects, as sold from defatted cake after supercritical CO2/ethanol extraction (SFE) had cadmium higher at 281 µg/kg, against 31.5 µg/kg for defatted cake after supercritical CO2/ethanol extraction (SFE) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/cuestaramos2024-edible-insects-defatted-cakes-metals|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-edible-insects" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-edible-insects" data-question="How do heavy metals get into edible insects?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into edible insects?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, edible insects from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than edible insects from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ajdini B, Biancarosa I, Illuminati S, Annibaldi A, Girolametti F, Fanelli M, Massi L, Truzzi C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements">Novel Food Safety Evaluation: Potentially Toxic Elements in Acheta domesticus (House Cricket) Reared on Seaweed-Enriched Diets</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Molecules 2025, 30, 3958</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Edible insects, as sold from trial 1 control diet, 0% Palmaria palmata (Ctrl-PP) (experiment) had lead higher at 18 µg/kg, against 14 µg/kg for trial 2 control diet, 0% Ascophyllum nodosum (Ctrl-AN) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ajdini B, Biancarosa I, Illuminati S, Annibaldi A, Girolametti F, Fanelli M, Massi L, Truzzi C · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements">Novel Food Safety Evaluation: Potentially Toxic Elements in Acheta domesticus (House Cricket) Reared on Seaweed-Enriched Diets</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Molecules 2025, 30, 3958</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ajdini2025-house-cricket-seaweed-diet-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-types-of-edible-insects-have-the-lowest-levels" data-anchor="which-types-of-edible-insects-have-the-lowest-levels" data-question="Which types of edible insects have the lowest levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which types of edible insects have the lowest levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

For lead, the HMI reference median was lowest for edible insects, frozen (34 µg/kg) and highest for edible insects, powder or ground (69 µg/kg); forms differ in water content, so this compares foods as sold or eaten, not uptake.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2024-house-cricket-frozen-dried-powder-novel-food|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA NDA Panel, Turck D, Bohn T, Cámara M, Castenmiller J, De Henauw S, Hirsch-Ernst KI, Jos Á, Maciuk A, Mangelsdorf I, McNulty B, Naska A, Pentieva K, Siani A, Thies F, Aguilera-Gómez M, Cubadda F, Frenzel T, Heinonen M, Neuhäuser-Berthold M, Knutsen HK, Poulsen M, Prieto Maradona M, Schlatter JR, Siskos A, van Loveren H, Azzollini D, McArdle HJ · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2024-house-cricket-frozen-dried-powder-novel-food">Safety of frozen, dried and powder forms of house crickets (Acheta domesticus) as a novel food pursuant</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2024;22:e9101</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2024-house-cricket-frozen-dried-powder-novel-food">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2026-house-cricket-spray-dried-powder-novel-food|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA NDA Panel, Turck D, Bohn T, Cámara M, Castenmiller J, De Henauw S, Jos Á, Maciuk A, Mangelsdorf I, McNulty B, Naska A, Pentieva K, Siani A, Thies F, Aguilera-Gómez M, Frenzel T, McArdle HJ, Moldeus P, Neuhäuser-Berthold M, Schlatter JR, van Loveren H, Favata A, Rivero-Pino F, Ververis E, Hirsch-Ernst KI · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2026-house-cricket-spray-dried-powder-novel-food">Safety of Acheta domesticus (house cricket) spray-dried powder as a Novel food pursuant to <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-origins-or-products-of-edible-insects-measured-lowest" data-anchor="which-origins-or-products-of-edible-insects-measured-lowest" data-question="Which origins or products of edible insects measured lowest?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which origins or products of edible insects measured lowest?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In one study, lead across 17 groups of edible insects ranged from 10 µg/kg (CJ22, labeled origin Finland, insect-based food, 7.5% insect) to 160 µg/kg (CJ17, labeled origin Mexico, insect-based food, 73% insect); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/sanonofre2024-online-edible-insects-trace-elements|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">San Onofre N, Vie D, Soriano JM, Soler C · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/sanonofre2024-online-edible-insects-trace-elements">Presence of Trace Elements in Edible Insects Commercialized through Online E-Commerce Platform</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics 2024, 12, 741</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/sanonofre2024-online-edible-insects-trace-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, lead across 16 groups of edible insects ranged from 6.03 µg/kg (Worms 5, origin Toulouse, France, French market/online) to 107 µg/kg (Ants 1, origin Columbia, French market/online); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/holowaty2024-french-online-edible-insects-elements|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Holowaty Y, Leufroy A, Mazurais C, Beauchemin D, Jitaru P · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/holowaty2024-french-online-edible-insects-elements">Multi-Elemental Analysis of Edible Insects, Scorpions, and Tarantulas from French (Online) Market and Human Health Risk Assessment Due to Their Consumption: A Pilot Study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods 2024, 13, 2353</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/holowaty2024-french-online-edible-insects-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
